HAR Extractor user guide

HAR Extractor opens the network recordings that browsers save as .har files. It shows every request in the recording, points out passwords, tokens and other secrets inside them, and exports clean copies you can safely send to a customer, a colleague or a support team.

Everything happens inside your browser, on your computer. The file is never uploaded, and the page is built so that it cannot connect to the internet at all.

Getting started

What you need

Keep two files together in the same folder:

  • har-extractor.html, the app
  • user-guide.html, this guide

Double-click har-extractor.html to open it in your usual browser. It works in current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, Brave and Vivaldi on Windows, macOS and Linux. There is nothing to install and no account to create.

Opening a HAR file

Either drag a .har file onto the window, or click Choose HAR file. Once a file is open you can drop another one anywhere on the page, or use Open file in the top bar (Ctrl O, or Cmd O on a Mac) to replace it.

A file with a few hundred requests opens instantly. Very large captures (100 MB or more) take a few seconds. The table appears first, and the scan for sensitive data finishes in the background; you can work while it runs.

To clear the file from the page, click the × beside its name in the top bar. Closing the browser tab does the same.

Saving a HAR file from a browser

If a customer needs to send you a capture, these are the steps to give them:

  1. Open the website, then open the developer tools: press F12, or Cmd Option I on a Mac.
  2. Choose the Network tab. Tick Preserve log (Chrome and Edge) or Persist Logs (Firefox) so that nothing is lost when the page changes.
  3. Reload the page, then repeat the steps that show the problem.
  4. Save the recording:
    • Chrome and Edge: click the download arrow at the top of the Network tab, labelled Export HAR. Recent versions offer two choices: the sanitised one leaves out cookies and login headers, the other includes everything. Either opens in HAR Extractor; for login problems you may need the complete one.
    • Firefox: right-click any request and choose Save All As HAR.
    • Safari: enable the Develop menu in Safari's settings first, then click Export in the Network tab.
HAR files contain secrets.

A recording includes cookies, login tokens and anything typed into forms on the page, including passwords. Treat every HAR file like a password, and only pass one on after making a sanitised copy (see Exporting).

The screen at a glance

  1. File name. The open file with its size and number of requests. The × closes it.
  2. Capture timeline. Every request drawn as a bar from left (start of the recording) to right (end). Colours show the type of request; red bars are errors. Drag across it to focus on a moment in time.
  3. Summary bar. Totals for the requests you are looking at. Some values are buttons: click errors, over 1 s or sensitive values to jump straight to those requests.
  4. Filters. Switch between the request list and the sensitive data list, search, and narrow the list by type, status, domain or page.
  5. Request table. One row per request. Click a column heading to sort by it; click again to reverse the order.
  6. Detail panel. Everything about the selected request, split into tabs, plus buttons to copy it as a command or save its response.
  7. Top bar actions. Mask sensitive data, Privacy rules, Export, Open file, the shortcut list (?) and the light or dark theme switch.

Reading the request table

ColumnWhat it shows
#The request's position in the original file. It never changes, so it is a reliable way to refer to a request ("see request #42").
MethodGET, POST, PUT, DELETE and so on.
StatusThe HTTP status code. Green is success, amber is a 4xx client error, red is a 5xx server error. failed means no response arrived at all: the request was blocked, cancelled or the connection broke.
NameThe last part of the address, followed by the website it came from in grey. Hover to see the full address.
TypeFetch/XHR (data requests), Doc (pages), JS, CSS, Img, Font, Media, WS (WebSockets) or Other.
SizeBytes sent over the network, including headers. Hover for the uncompressed size of the content.
TimeHow long the request took from start to finish.
WaterfallWhen the request ran compared with the others. The pale part is time spent waiting for the server; the solid end is the download.
●The request contains sensitive data. A filled dot means at least one high-risk value (a password, token or key); a ring means only medium or low-risk values.

On narrower windows the Type, Size and Waterfall columns are hidden to make room. Drag the divider between the table and the detail panel to change their widths; the app remembers your choice.

On a phone or small screen

The layout stacks vertically. Tapping a request opens its details over the whole screen; the back arrow returns to the list. The filter chips scroll sideways.

Finding the requests you need

All filters work together. The summary bar, the timeline and the export options always reflect what is currently shown, and Reset filters appears whenever anything is active.

Search box

Click the box or press /, then type. Plain words match anywhere in the address, method, status, type or content type. Combine as many terms as you like; a request must match all of them.

Type thisTo show
checkoutRequests containing "checkout"
-analyticsEverything except requests containing "analytics". A minus works in front of any term.
status:404Exactly status 404
status:5Any status starting with 5 (500, 502, 503, 504…)
method:postOnly POST requests
domain:api.example.comRequests to websites whose name contains this text
type:jsOne type: fetch, doc, js, css, img, font, media, ws or other
mime:jsonContent type contains "json"
larger:500k smaller:2kSize above or below a value. Use k, m or g for kilobytes, megabytes and gigabytes.
slower:1000 faster:50Took longer or shorter than this many milliseconds
id:42Request #42 only
"two words"An exact phrase

Example: method:post domain:api -status:2 shows every POST to an API address that did not succeed. Press Esc to clear the box.

Type and status chips

  • Type chips (Fetch/XHR, Doc, JS and so on) show one type at a time. Hold Shift, Ctrl or Cmd while clicking to combine several. The number on each chip is how many requests of that type the file contains.
  • Status chips (4xx, 5xx, Failed) add together, so you can select any mix. They only appear when the capture has such errors.
  • Click a selected chip again to turn it off.

Domain, page and sensitive data

  • All domains lists every website in the recording, busiest first. Pick one to see only its requests.
  • When the recording covers more than one page visit, a page list appears next to it.
  • Has sensitive data keeps only requests marked with a ●.

Focusing on a moment with the timeline

  • Drag across the timeline to keep only requests that were running in that window. The waterfall column zooms to match, which makes slow stretches easy to read.
  • Click a single bar to select that request.
  • Click Show all on the timeline, or Reset filters, to see the whole recording again.
  • The dashed vertical line marks the selected request.

Sorting

Click any column heading. Size, Time and the sensitive data column sort largest first; click again for the reverse. Sorting by Time is the quickest way to find what slowed a page down; sorting by the ● column brings the riskiest requests to the top.

Inspecting a request

Click a row, or move through the list with ↑ and ↓. The detail panel shows the method, status and full address at the top, with tabs underneath. Tabs only appear when they have something to show; Payload and Cookies are absent for requests without them.

Overview
Address, status, protocol (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3), server IP address, type, start time, duration, sizes, any redirect target, cache use, priority, and what started the request (the "initiator") when the browser recorded it.
Headers
Every request and response header, in the order they were sent. Sensitive values are highlighted.
Payload
The query string (the part of the address after ?) split into separate values, and the request body for POST and PUT requests. Form submissions are shown field by field; JSON is neatly formatted (untick Format JSON to see it exactly as sent).
Response
What the server sent back. JSON is formatted, images are previewed, and other binary files (fonts, PDFs, archives) show their first bytes in hexadecimal. HTML, JavaScript and SVG are shown as plain text and never run. If a body is larger than 1.5 MB, the first part is shown with a Show everything link.
Cookies
Cookies sent with the request and cookies set by the response, with their attributes (domain, path, expiry, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite).
Timings
How the time was spent, phase by phase. See below.
Sensitive data
Everything the privacy rules found in this request, and where. The red number on the tab is the count.
Raw
The request's complete entry from the HAR file, exactly as recorded. With masking on, it shows the cleaned version that would go into a sanitised export.

Understanding timings

PhaseWhat it means, and what a large value usually points to
Queued or blockedWaiting in the browser before it could start. Large values usually mean too many requests to the same server at once.
DNS lookupTurning the website name into an IP address. Slow DNS points to the visitor's resolver or the domain's nameservers.
ConnectingOpening the network connection, including the TLS handshake.
TLS handshakeThe secure-connection part of connecting. It is already counted inside Connecting.
SendingUploading the request. Almost always tiny unless a large file is being sent.
Waiting (TTFB)Time to first byte: the server thinking. Large values here point at the server, its application or its database.
DownloadingReceiving the response. Large values mean a big file or a slow connection.

n/a means the phase did not happen, which is normal: DNS and connecting are skipped when the browser reuses an existing connection.

Copying and saving

  • Copy cURL copies a command that repeats the request from a terminal. Paste it into Linux, macOS or Windows Terminal to test a server directly.
  • Copy fetch copies the same request as JavaScript, ready for the browser console.
  • Copy URL copies the full address.
  • Save response saves the response body as a file with a sensible name and extension.
Copies include secrets unless masking is on.

A copied cURL command usually carries the user's login cookie or token. If you plan to paste it anywhere others can see, switch on Mask sensitive data first. The confirmation message always tells you which kind of copy you made.

Sensitive data and masking

As soon as a file opens, HAR Extractor checks every address, header, cookie, form field and body (including bodies the browser stored in base64) against the privacy rules. Anything that matches is underlined in raspberry wherever it appears.

Highlighting and masking

Turn on Mask sensitive data in the top bar, or press M. While masking is on, every sensitive value on screen is replaced with your label, and so is everything you copy or save from the detail panel. This is ideal for screen sharing, screenshots, or walking a customer through a capture on a call.

Masking keeps the useful structure visible. Cookie names stay, so sid=[REDACTED]; theme=[REDACTED] still tells you which cookies were sent, and authorisation headers keep their scheme, as in Bearer [REDACTED].

The sensitive data list

Click Sensitive data next to Requests (or the sensitive values total in the summary bar) to see every finding in one list, highest risk first. Each row shows the request number, risk level, what kind of value it is, exactly where it was found, and the value with its middle hidden.

  • Click a row to open that request on its Sensitive data tab.
  • Tick Show full values to see the complete values, for example to confirm a token belongs to a test account.
  • The list follows your filters, so you can check a single domain or time window.
  • Export findings saves the list (see Exporting).

Risk levels

  • High: could give someone access to an account or system, such as passwords, tokens, API keys, private keys and card numbers.
  • Medium: session data such as cookie values.
  • Low: personal details such as email and IP addresses.

Privacy rules

Click Privacy rules in the top bar to decide what counts as sensitive and how it is replaced. Your choices are saved in this browser and apply to the highlights, masking and every export. Click Apply and rescan to use them; Cancel discards changes.

The replacement label

  • Choose [REDACTED], [SENSITIVE DATA], or type your own label of up to 40 characters, such as [HIDDEN] or ***.
  • Tick Add the kind of data to the label to get labels like [REDACTED:jwt], [REDACTED:cookie] or [REDACTED:email]. This helps the reader of a cleaned file understand what was removed without seeing it.
  • Scan request and response bodies is on by default. Turn it off only if a huge capture is slow to scan and you are not concerned about page content. Exports still clean bodies regardless.

Built-in rules

RuleWhat it catches
Sensitive headersAuthorization, API key, token and session headers, such as Authorization, X-Api-Key and X-Auth-Token
Cookie valuesValues in Cookie and Set-Cookie headers and cookie lists; names and attributes are kept
Sensitive parametersAddress and form values whose name looks like a password, token, key, session, code or signature, such as ?api_key=… or password=…
Secret JSON fieldsJSON values whose name looks like a secret, such as "password": "…" or "access_token": "…"
JSON Web TokensSigned tokens beginning eyJ, wherever they appear
Bearer and Basic credentialsAnything after Bearer, Basic, Token or Digest
Credentials in URLsuser:password@ inside an address
Private keysBlocks starting -----BEGIN … PRIVATE KEY-----
Cloud and SaaS API keysKey formats from AWS, Google, GitHub, GitLab, Stripe, Slack, SendGrid, npm, Shopify, and sk- style AI service keys
Payment card numbers13 to 19 digit numbers that pass the card checksum (Luhn) test. Order numbers and phone numbers usually fail it and are left alone.
Email addressesAnything shaped like name@domain.tld
IPv4 addressesOff by default, because server addresses are usually needed when diagnosing. Turn it on before sharing captures from a customer's own network.

Your own rules

Add anything specific to a site or customer: account numbers, usernames, internal hostnames, staff names.

  1. Choose Text to match exact text, or Pattern for a JavaScript regular expression. For example, acct_[0-9]+ matches acct_ followed by any digits.
  2. Tick Ignore case if capital letters should not matter.
  3. Click Add rule, or press Enter. Remove a rule with its ×.

Testing rules before applying them

Paste any text into Test the rules and the result appears underneath as you type, using the settings in the window, even before you apply them. It is the quickest way to check that a pattern catches what you expect and nothing more.

Restore defaults resets the label, every rule and removes your own rules.

Exporting

Click Export in the top bar, or press E. Choose what to create on the left; the options and a live preview appear on the right.

Which export to choose

You want to…Choose
Explain a problem in a support ticket or emailDiagnostic report, Markdown or text
Give a developer or vendor the full capture to investigateSanitised HAR
Show a customer what secrets their capture containedSensitive data list
Analyse timings or sizes in Excel, LibreOffice or Google SheetsRequest table
Recover the actual files (images, scripts, JSON) a page loadedResponse files
Feed the results into another tool or an AI assistantDiagnostic report as JSON or Markdown

Options every export shares

  • Requests: All requests, only those Matching the filters (offered while filters are active), or just the Selected request. Filtering first is a good way to send someone only what matters.
  • Download saves to your usual downloads folder.
  • Save as… lets you pick the folder and name. It appears in Chrome, Edge and other Chromium browsers.
  • Copy puts the text on the clipboard, handy for pasting straight into a ticket. It is not available for ZIP files.
  • File names are made from the original file name, the export type and the date and time, so exports never overwrite each other.

Diagnostic report

A readable summary: the capture details, totals, status codes, request types, a per-domain breakdown, the ten slowest requests, a Requests worth a look section listing every error and slow request, then an index and full timings for each request. Request and response bodies and the original file name are never included.

  • Format: Markdown reads well in ticketing systems, GitHub, Notion and AI assistants; Text suits plain email; JSON is for other tools.
  • URLs: Origin only (just https://example.com), Origin and path, no query (the default), or Full URL with sensitive values replaced.
  • Slow request threshold: how many milliseconds count as slow (1000 by default).
  • Include headers: adds all headers, with sensitive values replaced.
  • Include sensitive data summary: counts of what was found, by type. Values are never written to a report.
  • Capture label and Notes for the reader: your own description of the problem, placed at the top.

Sanitised HAR

A complete HAR file with every sensitive value replaced by your label. It opens in any browser's developer tools (drag it onto the Network tab) and in other HAR viewers, so the recipient can investigate as if they had the original. Bodies stored in base64 are decoded, cleaned and re-encoded so they stay valid.

  • Remove response bodies: smaller files, and nothing from page content can slip through. Recommended when the recipient only needs headers and timings.
  • Indent the JSON: easier to read in a text editor, slightly larger.
  • Keep original values: skips cleaning entirely. Use it only to cut a large capture down to the requests that matter, for your own records. A warning appears while it is ticked.

Sensitive data list

Every finding with its request number, risk level, type, location and masked value, as Markdown, text, JSON or CSV. Ticking Include full values writes the secrets themselves into the file; a warning reminds you to keep such a file private.

Request table

A CSV file with one row per request: start time, method, status, type, content type, host, address, protocol, duration, sizes, every timing phase and the number of sensitive values. Sensitive values in addresses are replaced unless you untick the option. Cells that a spreadsheet might treat as a formula are made safe automatically.

Response files

A ZIP file with every captured response body saved as a real file, in folders by website and path, plus _manifest.csv listing what each file is and where it came from.

  • Replace sensitive values in text files cleans HTML, JSON, JavaScript, CSS and other text. Images, fonts and other binary files are kept exactly as recorded.
  • Compress makes a smaller ZIP and takes a little longer for big captures.

Only responses the browser actually recorded can be included. Browsers often leave out bodies of large files, media and requests served from cache.

Always review before sharing.

The rules catch the common kinds of secret, but no automatic check can know every format a website uses. Open the export, search it for anything specific to the account involved (a username, a customer number), and add a custom rule for anything that slipped through.

Common tasks

Send a customer's capture to a developer or hosting provider

  1. Open the customer's HAR file.
  2. Click the sensitive values total and look through the list to see what the capture contains.
  3. In Privacy rules, add custom rules for the customer's username, email or account number, and turn on IPv4 addresses if the capture came from their own network. Click Apply and rescan.
  4. Optionally filter to the requests that matter, for example domain:theirsite.com.
  5. Export, Sanitised HAR, choose the request scope, then Download.
  6. Open the new file in HAR Extractor once more: the sensitive values total should now be zero.

Find out why a page is slow

  1. Look at the timeline. A long gap, or one bar much longer than the rest, shows where the time went.
  2. Click the over 1 s total, or sort by Time.
  3. Open the slowest request's Timings tab. A long Waiting (TTFB) points to the server or application (for example a slow plugin or database query). A long Downloading points to a large file. Long DNS or Connecting points to DNS or the network.
  4. Check the Size column for unexpectedly large images or scripts.
  5. Export a diagnostic report in Markdown with a capture label and notes, and attach it to your ticket.

Track down failing requests

  1. Click the errors total. It selects the 4xx, 5xx and Failed chips together.
  2. Open each error. The Response tab often contains the server's own error message.
  3. For failed requests, the browser received no answer: look for ad blockers, security software, mixed content (http on an https page), CORS problems or a server that dropped the connection.
  4. Use Copy cURL with masking off to repeat a request from your terminal, and see whether it fails outside the browser too.

Check a HAR file is safe before sending it on

  1. Open the file. If the sensitive values total is zero, the built-in rules found nothing.
  2. Turn on Mask sensitive data and use the Raw tab on a few requests to see what a cleaned copy would contain.
  3. Search for anything personal you know about the account in question.

Troubleshooting

"This file is not valid JSON" or "has no log.entries list"

The file is not a HAR file, or it was cut short while saving. Ask for the capture to be exported again, and check the file ends with a closing }. Some tools save a ZIP or a .saz file instead; those need converting to HAR first.

The file is too large to open

Browsers limit how much text a page can hold, usually somewhere between 500 MB and 1 GB. Ask for a shorter recording: clear the Network tab, then capture only the steps that show the problem.

A response says "was not captured in this HAR file"

The browser did not record that body. This is normal for large files, media, cached responses, redirects and requests that failed, and for captures where the page was still loading when the file was saved. Nothing is wrong with HAR Extractor; the data simply is not in the file.

Sizes show 0 B or a dash

The response came from the browser's cache, or the browser did not record a size. The Overview tab shows when a cache was used.

A request shows "failed" with 0 ms

No response arrived. Common causes are ad or privacy blockers, the user leaving the page, a CORS rejection, mixed content, or the server closing the connection. The HAR file records that it happened, not why.

Something sensitive was not highlighted

Add a custom rule for it in Privacy rules. If it is a common kind of secret that the built-in rules should recognise, it is worth noting so the rules can be improved in a future version.

Something harmless is highlighted

Turn off the rule responsible in Privacy rules (the Sensitive data tab names it). For example, if a site uses a code parameter for product codes, the Sensitive parameters rule will flag it. Leaving it highlighted is usually the safer choice.

Copy buttons say copying was blocked

Some browsers restrict the clipboard for files opened from disk. Select the text by hand and press Ctrl C, or in the Export window use Download instead.

There is no "Save as…" button

Firefox and Safari do not offer it to web pages. Use Download; most browsers can be set to ask where to save each download.

My settings disappeared

Privacy rules, the theme and the panel width are stored by your browser. A private window, a different browser or profile, or clearing the browser's site data starts with the defaults again.

The "Open HAR Extractor" link in this guide does not work

The guide and the app need to be in the same folder, with their original names: har-extractor.html and user-guide.html.

Privacy and security

  • Nothing leaves your computer. Files are read by the page in your browser. The app contains a security policy that forbids every kind of network connection, so it could not send data anywhere even by mistake.
  • Captured content cannot run. A HAR file may contain web pages and scripts, sometimes hostile ones. HAR Extractor only ever displays them as text, and its security policy allows only the app's own code to run, nothing else.
  • Nothing is stored. The capture is held in memory only while it is open. Closing it, or closing the tab, releases it. Only your preferences are saved.
  • No outside code. The app is a single self-contained file with no third-party libraries. Anyone can open it in a text editor to see exactly what it does.
  • Exports are made defensively. File names inside ZIP files cannot escape the folder they are unpacked into, and spreadsheet exports cannot trigger formulas.

The one thing no tool can do for you is judge what is sensitive for a particular customer. A quick review of each export before sharing it remains the best protection.
